title: The global incidence and diagnosis of fungal keratitis
article_subtype: Systematic epidemiological review with a global incidence estimate and an assessment of diagnostic evidence
clinical_background: Fungal keratitis is a severe corneal infection that can cause permanent visual impairment, blindness, or loss of the eye. It is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and often affects young agricultural or outdoor workers after ocular injury. More than 100 fungal species can cause the condition, although over 95% of infections are attributed to Fusarium spp, Aspergillus spp, and Candida spp. Its clinical features overlap with those of other corneal infections, making diagnosis difficult. Epidemiological data from Africa, Asia, and central and South America have been limited, and the global incidence had not been carefully estimated.
objectives: Assess the published evidence on the incidence of fungal keratitis.
Evaluate the most effective approaches to diagnosing fungal keratitis.
Estimate the global burden of fungal keratitis using the most reliable available data.
study_design: Review combining a systematic literature search on fungal keratitis epidemiology from Jan 1, 1946, to July 26, 2019, with separate searches of diagnostic studies. The authors used eligible epidemiological studies to estimate annual incidence by country, region, and globally.

population.description: Published studies of fungal keratitis and microbial keratitis, including 18 papers reporting fungal keratitis incidence in a defined population. Incidence rates per 100000 people were calculated for people aged 20–70 years. Diagnostic searches covered studies comparing methods for identifying fungal keratitis.
inclusion_criteria: For the incidence estimate, studies reporting fungal keratitis incidence in a defined population and receiving an adapted GRADE score of more than 2.
For the diagnostic assessment, papers in which both fungal-specific staining methods and culture were performed.
exclusion_criteria: Articles unrelated to fungal keratitis epidemiology, articles without original data, and articles reporting only bacterial keratitis were excluded from the epidemiological assessment.

comparators: Diagnostic comparisons encompassed clinical assessment, confocal microscopy, direct microscopy, histopathology, culture, and PCR.

primary: Estimated annual incidence of fungal keratitis globally and by region.
secondary: Fungal keratitis as a proportion of microbial keratitis.
Diagnostic performance of methods used to identify fungal keratitis.
Estimated incidence under the assumption that all culture-negative cases were fungal keratitis.

statistical_methods: The authors assigned regional incidence rates using data from a country in the region or one considered similar in climate and socioeconomic status. When a country had multiple incidence estimates, they calculated a weighted mean using studies less than 10 years old. They also calculated weighted means for the proportions of culture-negative and microscopy-negative cases, favouring studies from the past decade. Mixed bacterial and fungal infections were counted as fungal keratitis cases. Population denominators came from the UN World Population Prospects 2015 database. For sub-Saharan Africa, Kenyan county reports from 2013–17 were adjusted for incomplete records, with 45% of microbial keratitis cases assumed to be fungal. The authors examined associations between the fungal proportion of microbial keratitis and transformed values of gross domestic product per capita and distance from the equator using multivariable regression.
quality_assessment_tool: An adapted GRADE score assessing diagnostic accuracy, study size using a cutoff of >30 cases, study decade, and reporting of fungal keratitis as a proportion of microbial keratitis.
interpretation: The authors estimate at least 1051787 new cases of fungal keratitis annually worldwide (736251–1367323), with the greatest burden in Asia and Africa. If every culture-negative case is assumed to be fungal, the estimate rises to 1480916 (1036641–1925191); the authors caution that some of those cases could instead be bacterial. They consider the burden likely underestimated because diagnostic methods miss infections and some affected people never reach care. Delayed diagnosis and limited access to effective treatment contribute to blindness and eye removal.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors state that a global annual incidence had not previously been estimated. Earlier reports showed substantial differences between countries and suggested that the proportion of microbial keratitis attributable to fungi might be increasing, but their observation periods were too disparate for pooled analysis. The authors’ estimates of severe ocular outcomes draw on case series from Pakistan, east Africa, Germany, and the UK, rather than on a direct global outcome measurement.
clinical_implications: Early identification can prevent irreversible corneal damage and improve the prospect of recovery; advanced infection can be difficult to treat and may lead to blindness or loss of the eye.
Clinical findings alone cannot reliably distinguish fungal keratitis from other corneal infections, making diagnostic testing important when available.
Negative microscopy or culture does not reliably exclude fungal keratitis because both methods have limited sensitivity.

The authors estimate that 94753–115810 eyes are surgically removed each year and predict, using outcomes from the Pakistan study for low-income and middle-income countries, that 610821 eyes become blind annually because of fungal keratitis.
practice_implications: For suspected fungal keratitis, obtain a detailed history of symptoms, preceding events, and risk factors; examine for ocular and systemic defects and manage identified defects to reduce recurrence.
Perform appropriate in-vivo or in-vitro testing when possible rather than relying solely on clinical appearance.

Obtain corneal material from the ulcer base and edges for direct microscopy and culture; use both methods whenever possible. The authors recommend Gram stain, calcofluor-white preparation, and either potassium hydroxide or lactophenol cotton blue stained preparations for microscopy.
Avoid excessive corneal scraping: a cited study advised against it because of the risk of scarring and subsequent deterioration in visual acuity.
Use microscopy alongside culture rather than waiting for culture alone, since fungal growth and identification can delay treatment.
The authors call for a simple, inexpensive point-of-care diagnostic method and affordable treatment to be available globally.
limitations: Country incidence estimates rest on sparse epidemiological evidence from Africa, Asia, and Latin America; estimates for some regions were extrapolated from countries considered similar in climate or socioeconomic status.
Within-country differences related partly to climate and occupational exposure are likely, but available data generally do not permit their formal estimation.
Most underlying studies relied on microscopy and culture, which can miss fungal infections; the authors report culture sensitivity of 73% at best.

People in remote rural communities may not seek professional care because of treatment costs, lost earnings, difficulty obtaining an escort, or travel distance, leaving cases outside the underlying data.
Most studies were conducted at tertiary facilities, where referrals and severe disease could make fungal keratitis disproportionately represented.

The higher incidence scenario assumes that all cases negative on both microscopy and culture were fungal, although some could have been bacterial; the true cause of many such cases cannot be established with methods available in most settings.
Differences between fungal pathogens and laboratories in culture sensitivity prevented the authors from mapping apparent regional differences in fungal causes.
Disparate time periods prevented pooled statistical analysis of a possible increase in the fungal share of microbial keratitis.
strengths: For sub-Saharan Africa, the estimate drew on real-world Kenyan data that the authors state were supported by local experience in Malawi.
open_questions: The cause of a substantial proportion of clinically suspected infections with negative microscopy and culture remains uncertain.
Whether the fungal proportion of microbial keratitis is increasing cannot be established from the available, temporally disparate reports.
The future role of IVCM in low-resource settings remains uncertain because of its cost and requirement for specialist training.
future_directions: Develop an inexpensive, straightforward point-of-care diagnostic method for fungal keratitis.
Improve global access to affordable treatment and the diagnostic facilities and skills needed for corneal scraping, fungal microscopy, culture, and identification.

tables.title: Estimated yearly incidence of fungal keratitis by UN region and source
tables.summary: The estimated yearly burden is greatest in Asia, at 939 895 cases, and lowest in Europe, at 99 cases. The worldwide estimate is 1 051 787 cases annually, corresponding to 23·6 per 100 000 people.

main_conclusion: The authors estimate that fungal keratitis affects more than a million people each year, and probably 1·4 million if culture-negative cases in high-incidence areas are usually fungal. Because delayed diagnosis and limited access to treatment contribute to blindness and eye loss, they call for a point-of-care diagnostic method and affordable treatment worldwide.
narrative_summary:
This Review assessed the epidemiology and diagnosis of fungal keratitis and estimated its global burden using a systematic literature review covering Jan 1, 1946, to July 26, 2019. The epidemiology search yielded 187 studies from 50 countries for detailed analysis; 18 papers reported incidence in a defined population and informed the geographic estimates. The authors calculated a minimum worldwide incidence of 1051787 cases annually (736251–1367323), with the highest estimated burdens in Asia and Africa. If every culture-negative case were assumed to be fungal, the estimate increased to 1480916 cases (1036641–1925191); the authors caution that some bacterial infections can also be culture-negative.

Clinical findings alone cannot reliably distinguish fungal keratitis from other corneal infections. The Review advises corneal sampling for microscopy and culture whenever possible, while noting that both methods can miss infection. Calcofluor-white with fluorescence microscopy was more sensitive than potassium hydroxide in the cited comparisons; culture can delay diagnosis because fungal growth generally takes 48–72 h and occasionally longer. The authors identify late presentation, scarce diagnostic capacity and poor availability of antifungal eye drops as barriers to preserving sight. They conclude that earlier diagnosis and access to affordable treatment are needed to reduce blindness and eye loss.

document_sections.heading: The global incidence and diagnosis of fungal keratitis
document_sections.content: Fungal keratitis is a serious corneal infection that frequently causes blindness or loss of the eye. It is most common in tropical and subtropical climates and often affects young agricultural workers with low socioeconomic status. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can protect vision. This Review examines diagnostic evidence and estimates worldwide burden through a systematic literature review covering January, 1946 to July, 2019. An adapted GRADE score assessed incidence studies. In the summary, 116 studies reported fungal keratitis as a proportion of microbial keratitis, and 18 reported incidence in a defined population. The estimated minimum annual incidence was 1051787 cases (736251–1367323), with the highest rates in Asia and Africa. Assigning every culture-negative case to fungal keratitis increased the estimate to 1480916 cases (1036641–1925191). In three case series, eye removal affected 8–11% of patients; the summary extrapolates this to 84143–115697 eyes lost annually. Because the condition probably affects over a million people each year, countries need affordable treatment and a simple, inexpensive diagnostic method.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: More than 100 species can infect the cornea, although over 95% of fungal infections are attributed to Fusarium spp, Aspergillus spp, and Candida spp. Filamentous fungi predominate in tropical and subtropical climates, whereas yeast is more frequent in temperate climates; filamentous infections generally have a worse prognosis. Fungal keratitis is also called mycotic keratitis, keratomycosis, or oculomycosis. It can permanently impair sight or lead to loss of the eye, is often inadequately treated, and has high morbidity. Estimates attribute 20–60% of culture-positive corneal infections in tropical and subtropical climates to fungi. Corneal infections have been described as a silent epidemic, but its scale had not been carefully estimated. The illness usually develops subacutely, beginning with eye pain and followed by blurred vision, redness, tearing or discharge, and photophobia; ulceration and corneal opacity can follow, with endophthalmitis occurring less often. Most cases follow ocular trauma, often a minor injury involving organic material during outdoor or agricultural work. Plant and animal material, and even dust, have been implicated. Men are more susceptible than women in association with their greater participation in this work. One case series found nearly 4% of cases in children, although the vast majority occur in adults aged 20–50 years. Other reported predispositions to filamentous disease include previous ocular surgery, ocular surface disease, contact lenses, prior topical or systemic corticosteroids, and immunosuppression such as HIV/AIDS. Non-sterile traditional eye remedies, frequently made from plants, can introduce infection. In temperate settings, inadequate tear production or eyelid closure can predispose to candida and candida-like keratitis. Candida spp may complicate existing Herpes simplex keratitis or contact-lens-related corneal defects. Overnight lens wear and ineffective cleaning have been associated with fungal disease; among contact lens users, low socioeconomic status is linked to increased risk attributed to inadequate hygiene education and insufficient cleaning-solution use. Corneal perforation is common, occurs five to six times more often than with bacterial keratitis, and often necessitates evisceration. Consequences include impaired vision, blindness, loss of the globe, and disfigurement. The differential diagnosis encompasses fungal, bacterial, viral, amoebic, oomycete, and parasitic infection. Findings suggestive of filamentous fungi include a firm or dry raised slough, an irregular or feathery stromal infiltrate border, satellite infiltrates, an immune ring, and endothelial plaques; hypopyon may also occur. Overlapping presenting signs often prevent clinical distinction from other corneal infections. Definitive diagnosis requires corneal scraping for direct microscopy and culture; molecular testing and in-vivo confocal microscopy may help, and biopsy is sometimes needed. The absence of a point-of-care test is a major barrier to better outcomes. Despite extensive reporting of trends and risk factors, epidemiological research in Africa, Asia, and central and South America has been scarce. This Review aims to assess incidence evidence and diagnostic approaches and use the most reliable data to estimate global burden.

document_sections.heading: Key messages
document_sections.content: Microbial keratitis is a preventable cause of generally unilateral blindness and, sometimes, eye loss; the fungal form is usually harder to diagnose and has poorer outcomes than other microbial forms. Despite more than 3600 publications on microbial keratitis, annual fungal incidence had not been established. The Review estimates a minimum of 1 million cases yearly, increasing to over 1·4 million if culture-negative cases are classified as fungal. Tropical and subtropical countries have the highest annual incidence and the highest fungal-to-bacterial ratio among microbial keratitis cases, with male agricultural workers particularly affected. For diagnostic sensitivity, calcofluor-white with florescence microscopy outperforms potassium hydroxide, Giemsa, lactophenol cotton blue, and Gram stain. Fungal culture remains essential, and more than 100 fungal species have been implicated. Late diagnosis and poor treatment outcomes probably result in removal of about 100 000 eyes each year.

document_sections.heading: Search strategies
document_sections.content: The epidemiological systematic review searched Embase, MEDLINE, PubMed, CINAHL, and Cochrane from Jan 1, 1946, to July 26, 2019. Studies reporting incidence in defined populations were assessed with an adapted GRADE score covering diagnostic accuracy, sample size using a cutoff of >30 cases, decade of study with preference for more recent work, and reporting of fungal disease as a proportion of microbial keratitis. Scores of more than 2 qualified for the minimum global estimate. Regional rates were assigned from a country in the region or a country considered similar in climate and socioeconomic status. When a country had several rates, a weighted mean used studies less than 10 years old. Because every case series included keratitis without microbiological confirmation, potentially owing to previous treatment and imperfect microscopy and culture, the authors recorded each country's culture-negative and microscopy-negative proportions and calculated weighted means. Studies from the past decade were preferred; otherwise, the most recently reported proportion was used. Infections showing both bacteria and fungi on culture or smears were counted only as fungal because bacterial coinfection might follow fungal invasion. Rates per 100000 people used the UN World Population Prospects 2015 database for people aged 20 to 70 years, the age group predominantly affected. Sparse sub-Saharan African data prompted use of Kenyan county microbial-keratitis reports from 2013–17, adjusted for incomplete reporting. The authors assumed that 45% of those cases were fungal when estimating case counts and incidence per 100000 people. Separate MEDLINE searches sought comparisons of clinical diagnosis, confocal microscopy, microscopy, histopathology, culture, and PCR. Diagnostic studies were included only if they used fungal-specific staining and culture; references in identified papers extended the search.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: The epidemiology search found 3668 records; title and abstract screening selected 397 for full-text review. After duplicate removal, 241 unique manuscripts underwent eligibility assessment. The authors report excluding 59 full-text articles and specify 33 unrelated to fungal-keratitis epidemiology, 16 without original data, and seven concerning bacterial keratitis alone. Detailed analysis comprised 187 studies from 50 countries. In this section, 118 studies reported fungal cases as a proportion of microbial keratitis, while 18 measured incidence in defined populations and formed the basis for country, regional, and global estimates. The authors estimate 1051787 new cases worldwide each year; Asia and Africa have the highest estimated incidence and Europe the lowest. An assumed error of plus or minus 30% gives 736251–1367323 cases annually. Climate-related variation occurs within countries, illustrated by higher frequency in southern than northern areas of the USA and China. Only Chinese data were considered sufficiently robust to estimate this variation formally, and climatic boundaries there remain somewhat arbitrary. The regional table presents estimated annual cases, incidence per 100 000 people, and the sources used for extrapolation. The mean culture-negative proportion among included microbial-keratitis studies was 40·8% (14024/34257), ranging from 5% in Sierra Leone to 74·4% in Thailand. Treating every unconfirmed case as fungal raises estimated worldwide annual incidence to 1480916 cases (1036641–1925191). This assumption reflects the limited sensitivity of microscopy and culture, but some bacterial infections are also culture-negative, even if Gramstain-positive. Among 37 countries with estimates, the fungal proportion of microbial keratitis ranged from 1·0% in Spain to 60·0% in Vietnam. For repeated national estimates, studies younger than 10 years took precedence; multiple such studies were combined using a sample-size-weighted mean. Proportions above 25% tended to occur near the equator, but not invariably. The proportion with proven fungal disease had a significant negative relationship with logged gross domestic product per capita (p<0·001), although adjusted R² was only 34%. A multivariable regression examined that proportion against logged gross domestic product per capita and logged distance from the equator; its plotted relationships left substantial variability unexplained. Fusarium spp was the most frequently identified cause, followed by Aspergillus spp and Candida spp. Reported regional differences in species were not mapped because culture sensitivity differs by organism and laboratory. Repeated reports from some countries suggest an increasing fungal proportion over time, but disparate time blocks prevented formal pooling. Most studies had limitations. Conventional culture and smear methods likely missed infections: even expert culture has sensitivity of only 73% at best. Rural patients might never reach care because of treatment costs, lost earnings, lack of an escort, or distance. Conversely, tertiary referral centres might over-represent severe fungal infections, which do not respond to first-line anti-bacterial therapy. A stated strength is the use of Kenyan real-world data for sub-Saharan Africa, supported by local experience in Malawi.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Diagnosing fungal keratitis promptly can avert irreversible corneal damage and markedly improve the prospect of full recovery. Assessment starts with strong clinical suspicion and a thorough history of symptoms, preceding events, and risks. Clinicians should look carefully for local ocular and systemic defects and manage them to prevent recurrence. Blurred vision, pain, and tearing are shared with other infectious keratitides. Fungal symptoms usually last longer, typically 5–10 days, but duration is an unreliable discriminator.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis based on clinical presentation
document_sections.content: Detailed examination can inform diagnosis before microbiological results or when testing is unavailable. In low-resource settings, ophthalmologists may have to diagnose by slit-lamp findings and treat empirically; distinguishing fungi from bacteria is particularly difficult. A study by Thomas and colleagues used logistic regression and independently associated serrated margins, raised slough, and a colour other than yellow with fungal keratitis, while anterior-chamber fibrin independently indicated bacterial infection. Its diagnostic algorithm used three associated clinical signs; colour was excluded as too subjective. Pigmented ulcers nevertheless characterize some fungal infections caused by dematiaceous moulds. With serrated, feathery infiltrate margins and raised slough present but anterior-chamber fibrin absent, the algorithm gives an 89% likelihood of fungal infection. In another study, clinicians correctly distinguished fungal from bacterial keratitis in 66% of cases, but rarely predicted the fungal Gram stain, genus, or species accurately. Chronic filamentous infection may involve the entire cornea and resemble bacterial suppuration. Because clinical features lack specificity and clinical diagnostic sensitivity is low, appropriate in-vivo or in-vitro testing should be performed whenever possible. Clinical findings alone also make Acanthamoeba keratitis difficult to distinguish from fungal disease; uveitis, a ring infiltrate, an endothelial plaque, and corneal thinning warrant heightened suspicion of Acanthamoeba. Contact lens wear with poor hygiene and exposure to water containing amoebae are its most common predisposing factors. In patients without immunocompromise, microsporidial keratitis has a distinctive multifocal punctate pattern unlike fungal, bacterial, or Acanthamoeba disease. It is proportionally more common in immunocompromised patients and can produce deep ulcers. Pythium keratitis can resemble fungal disease through feathery margins but also has distinctive dot-like infiltrates beside the ulcer.

document_sections.heading: In-vivo confocal microscopy
document_sections.content: In-vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) is a non-invasive examination that can identify filamentous fungal structures and Acanthamoeba cysts in real time. Magnification is around ×500, with lateral resolution of 1 μm, allowing examination of corneal layers, cells, nuclei, and nerves even when oedema, inflammation, or fibrosis is present. Prospective diagnostic studies report fungal-keratitis sensitivity between 85% and 94% and specificity between 71% and 92%. Acquiring and interpreting images require expertise. Proposed differentiation of Aspergillous spp from Fusarium spp by branching angle has not yielded a convincing distinction. IVCM can rapidly detect fungal infection in most affected patients, including infection deep in the cornea that is difficult to sample. High cost and limited availability restrict its use, especially in low-income and middle-income countries; it is usually available only at a few centres in high-income countries. Although useful for fungal and Acanthamoeba keratitis, its resolution cannot confirm bacterial infection because bacteria are too small to visualize. The microscope contacts the eye and can cause discomfort, increased movement, and blurred images; good image quality requires substantial patient cooperation. Its future place in low-resource settings remains uncertain because of expense and specialist training needs.

document_sections.heading: Sample collection
document_sections.content: For microbiology, specimens are scraped from ulcer bases and margins with a sterile Kimura spatula, surgical blade, or hypodermic needle (21 or 23 gauge). Collection follows preservative-free local anaesthetic and precedes fluorescein. Multiple solid and liquid media and microscopy slides are inoculated in the clinic to detect different possible organisms. Spreading material thinly on slides aids visualization, while solid agar must not be punctured by sharp collection tools. Swabs usually yield too little fungal material because fungi tend to extend deep into the cornea. Although scraping removes necrotic tissue, one study cautioned against excessive scraping because scarring could subsequently worsen visual acuity.

document_sections.heading: Microscopy
document_sections.content: Direct examination of corneal smears rapidly separates fungal disease from other microbial infections and is considered a diagnostic gold standard: observed hyphae support starting antifungal treatment. Some stains can identify bacteria and amoebae at the same time. Recommended preparations are Gram stain, calcofluor-white, and either potassium hydroxide or lactophenol cotton blue; additional options include Giemsa, periodic acid Schiff, and Gomori methenamine silver stain. With trained microscopists, calcofluor-white and florescence microscopy is more sensitive for fungal disease than potassium hydroxide, which in turn exceeds lactophenol cotton blue. A 2010 comparison found fluorescence microscopy more sensitive but less specific than Giemsa staining. Direct microscopy is generally inexpensive, comparatively simple, rapid, and suitable for low-resource settings. Reported sensitivities are 61–94% for potassium hydroxide, 85% for lactophenol blue, and 36–50% for traditional Gram stain. Combining calcofluor-white with potassium hydroxide has produced sensitivity of 98·3%. Methylene blue might also permit rapid diagnosis, although calcofluor-white performs better. Gram stain remains valuable for detecting hyphae where other stains are unavailable. Staining artefacts can cause false positives, and uncommon fungal species may escape detection. Smears may distinguish yeasts from filamentous fungi and sometimes reveal pigmented dematiaceous fungi, but cannot alone identify fungal genera or species. Both microscopy and culture are therefore advised whenever feasible.

document_sections.heading: Culture
document_sections.content: Corneal scrapings are inoculated onto blood agar, chocolate agar, and Sabouraud dextrose agar in C-shaped streaks; given the small inoculum, growth is considered significant only within the streaked area. An Indian study comparing growth and cost reported fungal growth on 56% of blood agar, 46% of chocolate blood, and 43% of Sabouraud dextrose agar plates. Its authors concluded that blood and chocolate agar support some, but not every, causative fungus and are more cost-effective than Sabouraud dextrose agar. In settings with limited resources and prevalent disease, however, animal blood can be difficult to obtain. Sabouraud dextrose agar or potato dextrose agar is still advised for optimal growth and dependable identification of filamentous fungi. Liquid media such as brain–heart infusion and thioglycolate broths are commonly used to improve organism recovery and dilute the effects of prior antimicrobial treatment. Although smears and culture together constitute the current diagnostic gold standard, culture lacks sensitivity. The involvement of >100 species also demands substantial mycological expertise to identify pathogens promptly and exclude contaminants. Fungal growth usually takes 48–72 h, so reliance on culture alone delays diagnosis and microscopy is always advised. Less common species can require 2 weeks before absence of growth is confirmed; some specimens have taken up to 35 days to grow. Delayed diagnosis and treatment contribute to poor prognosis. Cultures still positive at 6 days of therapy indicated poor outcome. Corneal biopsy may be needed for microbiological diagnosis when other methods fail.

document_sections.heading: PCR
document_sections.content: Because culture has substantial limitations, molecular diagnostic methods have been developed. PCR is the preferred molecular tool, requires little specimen material, and has shown high sensitivity and specificity relative to smear stains and culture. In a 10-year retrospective non-randomised trial using specimens from 20 patients with confirmed fungal keratitis, PCR identified the causative species in 92·6% of cases, Gram stain and calcofluor-white preparations in 66·6%, and culture in 59·3%. Another study reported corresponding identification rates of 81·6%, 42·1%, and 68·4%. Its speed and accuracy have led some researchers to advocate widespread PCR use, but its present utility is limited in the low-resource settings bearing the greatest disease burden.

document_sections.heading: Ocular outcomes
document_sections.content: Four case series report outcomes outside randomised clinical trials. In a Pakistan series, 59% of eyes ended with vision worse than 6/60 and 11% of cases required evisceration. In east Africa, final vision was worse than 6/60 in 66% of eyes, corneal perforation occurred in 30%, and evisceration was required in 8%. A German series covering 2000–17 reported penetrating keratoplasty in 57% and enucleation in 9%. In the UK, 20% of eyes became blind, while 56% retained good vision (6/5–6/12). Extrapolating these outcomes, the authors calculate 94753–115810 eyes surgically removed each year; losses are probably higher where eye care is suboptimal. Applying the Pakistan outcomes to low-income and middle-income countries, they predict 610821 eyes becoming blind annually because of fungal keratitis.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors state that worldwide annual incidence had not previously been estimated. Sparse epidemiological evidence from Africa, Asia, and Latin America limits national estimates. Incidence probably varies within countries because of climate and occupational exposures, as occurs with bacterial keratitis. Limited sensitivity of fungal microscopy and culture means estimates derived from them are too low. Despite these limitations, the authors estimate over a million affected eyes annually and consider 1·4 million probable if culture-negative cases in high-incidence areas are usually fungal. They state that approximately 10% of eyes perforate or require removal and that over 60% of patients are left with mono-ocular blindness even after treatment; major improvements in eye health care are needed. Most reviewed epidemiological studies diagnosed microbial keratitis with both microscopy and culture, yet some clinically suspected cases were negative by both and treated empirically. The authors suspect fungi caused a substantial proportion of these negative cases, while acknowledging that this cannot currently be established in most settings. Good outcomes begin with high-quality clinical specimens and also depend on a trained, dedicated microbiology service. Initial management is medical; surgery may also be necessary. Medical care includes specific topical or systemic antifungal drugs and supportive measures such as cycloplegics. Topical 5% natamycin effectively manages 75% of corneas that are not severely affected and 60% of severely affected corneas; WHO now lists it as an essential medicine. Penetrating keratoplasty may be needed for medically refractory infection or later visual rehabilitation if donor tissue is available. In intractable disease with perforation and no donor cornea, evisceration is required. Delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes. A Tanzanian study reported a median hospital-presentation delay of 14 days, extending to 21 days when patients first visited another facility; a similar delay was reported in Uganda. Inadequate or inappropriate initial treatment is common, and extensive deep lesions may develop before patients seek care, leaving sight beyond preservation. Despite inclusion of natamycin eye drops on the WHO essential medicines list, antifungal eye drops remain poorly available. Facilities and skills for scraping, fungal microscopy, culture, and colony identification are scarce in most places. The most recent cited management guidelines were published in 2004 by the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. The disease likely affects over a million people yearly, of whom probably three quarters lose an eye or sight. Advanced disease is debilitating and difficult to treat, but early diagnosis and generic antifungal therapy usually make it treatable. The authors call for point-of-care diagnosis and worldwide access to affordable treatment.
